claim: Locomotion circuits developed in simple animals, and circuit motifs further evolved in higher animals.
source: Locomotion circuits developed in simple animals, and circuit motifs further evolved in higher animals.
evidence: This is a general statement about evolutionary development of locomotion circuits, presented as established knowledge in the field.

claim: The nematode Caenorhabditis elegans possesses one of the best-studied circuits for undulatory movement.
source: The nematode Caenorhabditis elegans possesses one of the best-studied circuits for undulatory movement.
evidence: This statement reflects established knowledge about C. elegans as a model organism for studying locomotion circuits.

claim: For 1/6th of the cholinergic motor neurons (MNs), the AS MNs, functional information is unavailable.
source: Yet, for 1/6th of the cholinergic motor neurons (MNs), the AS MNs, functional information is unavailable.
evidence: This claim establishes the knowledge gap that motivates the study, based on the state of the literature.

claim: AS MNs innervate muscles and other MNs asymmetrically, without complementary partners.
source: AS MNs differ, as they innervate muscles and other MNs asymmetrically, without complementary partners.
evidence: This is based on known anatomical connectivity from the wiring diagram.

claim: AS MNs generate asymmetric muscle activation, enabling navigation.
source: They generate asymmetric muscle activation, enabling navigation, and contribute to coordination of dorso-ventral undulation as well as anterio-posterior bending wave propagation.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study, supported by optogenetic and behavioral experiments shown in the manuscript.

claim: AS MNs contribute to coordination of dorso-ventral undulation.
source: They generate asymmetric muscle activation, enabling navigation, and contribute to coordination of dorso-ventral undulation as well as anterio-posterior bending wave propagation.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data from optogenetic manipulation and imaging.

claim: AS MNs contribute to anterio-posterior bending wave propagation.
source: They generate asymmetric muscle activation, enabling navigation, and contribute to coordination of dorso-ventral undulation as well as anterio-posterior bending wave propagation.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by experimental data showing disruption of wave propagation upon AS MN manipulation.

claim: AS MN activity correlated with forward and backward locomotion.
source: AS MN activity correlated with forward and backward locomotion, and they functionally connect to premotor interneurons (PINs) for both locomotion regimes.
evidence: This is supported by calcium imaging data in moving animals shown in Figure 5.

claim: AS MNs functionally connect to premotor interneurons (PINs) for both forward and backward locomotion regimes.
source: AS MN activity correlated with forward and backward locomotion, and they functionally connect to premotor interneurons (PINs) for both locomotion regimes.
evidence: This is supported by optogenetic stimulation and calcium imaging experiments shown in Figure 6.

claim: Electrical feedback from AS MNs via gap junctions may affect only backward PINs.
source: Electrical feedback from AS MNs via gap junctions may affect only backward PINs.
evidence: This is based on experimental data showing AS MN stimulation affects AVA but not AVB, and is presented as a speculative interpretation.

claim: Locomotion represents a basic component of many complex behaviors and is regulated by neuronal circuits that share similar properties in a wide variety of species, including humans.
source: Locomotion represents a basic component of many complex behaviors and is regulated by neuronal circuits that share similar properties in a wide variety of species, including humans (Guertin, 2012; Kiehn, 2011; Mullins et al., 2011).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Locomotion circuits can generate rhythmic motor patterns without sensory inputs, and therefore act as central pattern generators (CPGs).
source: These circuits, as shown in virtually all model systems studied, can generate rhythmic motor patterns without sensory inputs, and therefore act as central pattern generators (CPGs; Pearson, 1993).
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field, supported by a citation.

claim: In higher vertebrates CPGs are very complex systems and represent distributed networks made of multiple coupled oscillatory centers, grouping in pools as discrete operational units.
source: In higher vertebrates CPGs are very complex systems and represent distributed networks made of multiple coupled oscillatory centers, grouping in pools as discrete operational units (Fidelin et al., 2015; Kiehn et al., 2010; Rybak et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature on vertebrate CPGs.

claim: Motor neurons within the pool are able to integrate convergent inputs and are recruited and activated gradually, which underlies the variable changes in muscle tension that are necessary for movement.
source: Motor neurons (MNs) within the pool are able to integrate convergent inputs; they are recruited and activated gradually, which underlies the variable changes in muscle tension that are necessary for movement.
evidence: This is established knowledge about motor neuron function in vertebrate locomotion.

claim: Premotor interneurons modulate the patterns of MN activity and coordinate the CPGs.
source: Overlaid on these circuits are interactions with (and among) premotor interneurons (PINs), which modulate the patterns of MN activity and coordinate the CPGs (Goulding, 2009).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: In mammals, commissural interneurons (CIN) regulate activity of left and right CPGs, and may themselves act as rhythm generators.
source: In mammals, it is particularly the commissural interneurons (CIN) which regulate activity of left and right CPGs, and which may therefore themselves act as rhythm generators.
evidence: This is established knowledge about mammalian locomotor circuits, with speculative element about rhythm generation.

claim: Commissural interneurons can be excitatory (e.g. CINei of the mouse) or inhibitory (e.g. CINi).
source: Such neurons are often excitatory (e.g. CINei of the mouse; Kiehn, 2016), but can also be inhibitory (e.g. CINi), while others act as electrical connectors or activity 'sinks' for CPGs and motor neuron pools.
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work on mouse locomotor circuits.

claim: Ipsilateral V2a interneurons in zebrafish are retrogradely recruited by motor neurons to modulate their activity.
source: Examples are ipsilateral V2a interneurons in zebrafish, which are retrogradely recruited by motor neurons (Song et al., 2016) to modulate their activity.
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work on zebrafish.

claim: Motor neurons provide feedback to the CPG during drug-induced locomotor-like activity in the neonatal mouse.
source: A similar effect of motor neurons providing feedback to the CPG was recently shown for drug-induced locomotor-like activity in the neonatal mouse (Falgairolle et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Vertebrates and invertebrates share similar principles in locomotion circuits despite differences in forms of locomotion and anatomy of neural circuits.
source: Despite the difference in the forms of locomotion and anatomy of neural circuits between vertebrates and invertebrates, they share similar principles.
evidence: This is a general statement based on comparative neuroscience knowledge.

claim: How complex vertebrate locomotion circuits operate and how they developed from more simple ones is not understood.
source: Yet, how complex vertebrate locomotion circuits operate and how they developed from more simple ones is not understood, thus a comprehensive analysis of invertebrate circuits is a prerequisite to this goal.
evidence: This identifies a knowledge gap in the field.

claim: The relative simplicity of invertebrate nervous systems has helped to develop concepts that guide our understanding of how complex neuronal networks operate.
source: The relative simplicity of invertebrate nervous systems has helped to develop concepts that guide our understanding of how complex neuronal networks operate (Marder et al., 2005; Selverston, 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: C. elegans is a nematode with only 302 neurons in the hermaphrodite.
source: C. elegans is a nematode with only 302 neurons in the hermaphrodite.
evidence: This is established anatomical knowledge about C. elegans.

claim: A largely reconstructed wiring diagram of C. elegans neural circuits exists.
source: A largely reconstructed wiring diagram of its neural circuits (Varshney et al., 2011; White et al., 1986) and various tools for imaging and (opto)genetic interrogation of circuit activity (Fang-Yen et al., 2015; Leifer et al., 2011; Nagel et al., 2005; Stirman et al., 2011) render C. elegans a useful model to study fundamental principles of the neuronal control of behavior.
evidence: This is supported by citations to the connectome papers.

claim: C. elegans moves by generating waves of dorso-ventral bends along its body.
source: C. elegans moves by generating waves of dorso-ventral bends along its body.
evidence: This is established knowledge about C. elegans locomotion.

claim: C. elegans undulations predominantly lead to forward movement, which is occasionally interrupted by brief backing episodes.
source: These predominantly lead to forward movement, which is occasionally interrupted by brief backing episodes, the frequency of which is modulated by sensory responses (Cohen and Sanders, 2014; Gjorgjieva et al., 2014; Pierce-Shimomura et al., 2008; Zhen and Samuel, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work on C. elegans locomotion.

claim: The animal's undulations are controlled by neural circuits in the head and VNC.
source: The animal's undulations are controlled by neural circuits in the head and VNC.
evidence: This is established knowledge about C. elegans locomotor control.

claim: Head motor/interneurons exhibit Ca2+ oscillations during alternating head bending.
source: The core components of the motor circuits in C. elegans include head motor/interneurons that exhibit Ca2+ oscillations during alternating head bending (Hendricks et al., 2012; Shen et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Bending motions may be transmitted to the remainder of the body in part by proprioceptive feedback.
source: The bending motions may be transmitted to the remainder of the body in part by proprioceptive feedback (Wen et al., 2012), with contribution also by gap junctions (Xu et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work, with speculative language ('may be').

claim: Gap junctions contribute to transmission of bending motions to the remainder of the body.
source: The bending motions may be transmitted to the remainder of the body in part by proprioceptive feedback (Wen et al., 2012), with contribution also by gap junctions (Xu et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Rhythm generators in the VNC play a role in oscillatory activity during locomotion of C. elegans.
source: Furthermore, rhythm generators in the VNC were shown to play a role in oscillatory activity during locomotion of C. elegans (Fouad et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Motor neurons in the body are found in ensembles or subcircuits, repeating 6 times from the 'neck' to the tail of the animal.
source: In the body, motor neurons are found in ensembles or subcircuits, repeating 6 times from the 'neck' to the tail of the animal, containing one or two neurons of each class (6 – 13 neurons found in the individual classes, with 11 AS MNs; Haspel and O'Donovan, 2011; White et al., 1986).
evidence: This is supported by citations to anatomical studies.

claim: There are 11 AS MNs in C. elegans.
source: In the body, motor neurons are found in ensembles or subcircuits, repeating 6 times from the 'neck' to the tail of the animal, containing one or two neurons of each class (6 – 13 neurons found in the individual classes, with 11 AS MNs; Haspel and O'Donovan, 2011; White et al., 1986).
evidence: This is supported by citations to anatomical studies.

claim: PINs integrate inputs from sensory and other interneurons, and relay their activity in a gating fashion.
source: Upstream of the motor neurons are PINs which integrate inputs from sensory and other interneurons, and that relay their activity in a gating fashion: They are themselves not oscillatory, but set up- or down-states of the motor neurons, using gap junction and synaptic networks (Kawano et al., 2011), in a manner similar to the V2a interneurons of the fish (Song et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: PINs are not themselves oscillatory, but set up- or down-states of the motor neurons.
source: Upstream of the motor neurons are PINs which integrate inputs from sensory and other interneurons, and that relay their activity in a gating fashion: They are themselves not oscillatory, but set up- or down-states of the motor neurons, using gap junction and synaptic networks (Kawano et al., 2011), in a manner similar to the V2a interneurons of the fish (Song et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: The classes of MNs are distinguished by transmitter used (acetylcholine or GABA), ventral or dorsal innervation, and roles in forward or backward locomotion.
source: The classes of MNs are distinguished by transmitter used (acetylcholine or GABA), ventral or dorsal innervation, and roles in forward or backward locomotion (Von Stetina et al., 2005; Zhen and Samuel, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: The DA9 A-type MN generates intrinsic rhythmic activity by P/Q/N-type Ca2+ channels.
source: For example, the DA9 A-type MN was recently demonstrated to generate intrinsic rhythmic activity by P/Q/N-type Ca2+ channels, which is both attenuated and potentiated by activity of the reversal PIN AVA (Kawano et al., 2011; Gao et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: DA9 rhythmic activity is both attenuated and potentiated by activity of the reversal PIN AVA.
source: For example, the DA9 A-type MN was recently demonstrated to generate intrinsic rhythmic activity by P/Q/N-type Ca2+ channels, which is both attenuated and potentiated by activity of the reversal PIN AVA (Kawano et al., 2011; Gao et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Motor neurons, rather than interneurons, can be oscillators in C. elegans.
source: Thus, motor neurons, rather than interneurons, can be oscillators, demonstrating that different activities are compressed in the C. elegans motor circuit with its limited number of cells.
evidence: This is an inference based on the cited work on DA9 and general knowledge of C. elegans circuits.

claim: For the cholinergic AS MN class, representing one fifth of VNC cholinergic neurons, no physiological data is available.
source: However, for the cholinergic AS MN class, representing one fifth of VNC cholinergic neurons, surprisingly no physiological data is available.
evidence: This identifies the knowledge gap that motivates the study.

claim: AS MNs asymmetrically innervate only dorsal muscle and ventral inhibitory VD neurons.
source: Yet, these neurons are interesting in that they asymmetrically innervate only dorsal muscle and ventral inhibitory VD neurons.
evidence: This is based on the wiring diagram from previous anatomical studies.

claim: In contrast to other MN types, the AS MNs are innervated extensively by chemical synapses from both forward and reverse PINs.
source: Further, in contrast to other MN types, the AS MNs are innervated extensively by chemical synapses from both forward and reverse PINs, and they also form gap junctions with these cells (White et al., 1986).
evidence: This is based on the wiring diagram from previous anatomical studies.

claim: AS MNs form gap junctions with forward and reverse PINs.
source: Further, in contrast to other MN types, the AS MNs are innervated extensively by chemical synapses from both forward and reverse PINs, and they also form gap junctions with these cells (White et al., 1986).
evidence: This is based on the wiring diagram from previous anatomical studies.

claim: Stimulation of AS MNs distorts propagation of the body wave.
source: We reveal important roles of AS MNs in dorso-ventral and antero-posterior coordination of undulations during locomotion, as stimulation of AS MNs distorts, and inhibition blocks, propagation of the body wave.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by optogenetic experiments shown in the manuscript.

claim: Inhibition of AS MNs blocks propagation of the body wave.
source: We reveal important roles of AS MNs in dorso-ventral and antero-posterior coordination of undulations during locomotion, as stimulation of AS MNs distorts, and inhibition blocks, propagation of the body wave.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by optogenetic experiments shown in the manuscript.

claim: AS MNs act through excitation of dorsal muscles and inhibitory ventral VD motor neurons.
source: We show that AS MNs act through excitation of dorsal muscles and inhibitory ventral VD motor neurons.
evidence: This is supported by calcium imaging experiments in muscles shown in the manuscript.

claim: No promotor exclusively triggering expression in AS MNs is known.
source: Up to date, no promotor exclusively triggering expression in AS MNs is known.
evidence: This is a statement about the state of available genetic tools.

claim: The punc-17 promoter drives expression in all cholinergic neurons including the MNs in the VNC.
source: The punc-17 promoter (unc-17 encodes the vesicular acetylcholine transporter) drives expression in all cholinergic neurons including the MNs in the VNC.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the punc-17 promoter.

claim: Expression from punc-17 can be restricted to AS MNs by combining it with pacr-5 and punc-4 promoters driving dsRNA constructs.
source: In combination with pacr-5 (expression in DB and VB MNs) and punc-4 (expression in DA, VA and VC MNs), we could restrict expression of optogenetic tools to the AS MNs (Figure 1A,B): Briefly, broad expression from punc-17 was suppressed in the DB, VB, DA, VA and VC neurons by expressing dsRNA constructs targeting the optogenetic tool using pacr-5 and punc-4 promoters (Figure 1AI).
evidence: This is a methodological approach developed and validated in this study, shown in Figure 1.

claim: Expression along the VNC was restricted to AS MNs using the subtractive approach.
source: We verified that expression along the VNC was restricted to AS MNs, by imaging many animals (Figure 1B; Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is verified by imaging data shown in Figure 1B and Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Activation of ChR2 in all cholinergic neurons including VNC MNs leads to strong contraction of the worm body and coiling.
source: Activation of ChR2 in all cholinergic neurons including VNC MNs leads to strong contraction of the worm body and coiling (Zhang et al., 2007; Liewald et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Animals in which ChR2 was activated in AS MNs kept the ability to propagate the undulation.
source: Animals in which ChR2 was activated in AS MNs kept the ability to propagate the undulation, yet they displayed a distorted wave, deeper bending (Figure 1C,DI), and transiently reduced speed (Figure 1DII, III).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C and 1D.

claim: ChR2 activation in AS MNs causes deeper bending during locomotion.
source: Animals in which ChR2 was activated in AS MNs kept the ability to propagate the undulation, yet they displayed a distorted wave, deeper bending (Figure 1C,DI), and transiently reduced speed (Figure 1DII, III).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: ChR2 activation in AS MNs causes transiently reduced speed during locomotion.
source: Animals in which ChR2 was activated in AS MNs kept the ability to propagate the undulation, yet they displayed a distorted wave, deeper bending (Figure 1C,DI), and transiently reduced speed (Figure 1DII, III).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Photo-depolarization of AS MNs evoked body contraction.
source: Furthermore, photo-depolarization of AS MNs evoked body contraction, though contraction was reduced when compared to ChR2 activation of all VNC cholinergic MNs (Figure 1DIV,V).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Body contraction from AS MN depolarization was reduced when compared to ChR2 activation of all VNC cholinergic MNs.
source: Furthermore, photo-depolarization of AS MNs evoked body contraction, though contraction was reduced when compared to ChR2 activation of all VNC cholinergic MNs (Figure 1DIV,V).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: These behavioral phenotypes were blue-light dependent, and absent in transgenic animals raised without all-trans retinal (ATR).
source: These behavioral phenotypes were blue-light dependent, and absent in transgenic animals raised without all-trans retinal (ATR), the obligate ChR2 co-factor.
evidence: This is a control experiment demonstrating specificity of the optogenetic manipulation.

claim: Stimulation of AS MNs in small segments of the body led to a reduction of body length.
source: These manipulations neither caused marked disruption of the wave (Figure 1EII), nor did they reduce speed. However, they led to a reduction of body length (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A–C), most pronounced after stimulation of the anterior segment.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: Body length reduction was most pronounced after stimulation of the anterior segment.
source: These manipulations neither caused marked disruption of the wave (Figure 1EII), nor did they reduce speed. However, they led to a reduction of body length (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A–C), most pronounced after stimulation of the anterior segment.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: AS MN depolarization facilitates, but may not play an instructive role in generating the undulatory wave.
source: In sum, AS MN depolarization facilitates, but may not play an instructive role in generating the undulatory wave.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental results, with speculative language.

claim: During photostimulation of ChR2 in AS MNs, animals crawled in circles.
source: In contrast, during photostimulation of ChR2 just in AS MNs, animals crawled in circles (Figure 2AII; Figure 1—video 1)
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Circular crawling during AS MN stimulation was due to a bias of head bending towards the dorsal side.
source: This was due to a bias of head bending towards the dorsal side (Figure 2AIII–VI; Figure 1—figure supplement 3B), which led to a mild, but significant increase in average bending along the entire body (Figure 2AV, VI; this was stronger for AS::Chrimson animals, Figure 1—figure supplement 3E)
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A and Figure 1—figure supplement 3.

claim: Depolarization of AS MNs contributes to dorso-ventral coordination.
source: In sum, depolarization of AS MNs contributes to dorso-ventral coordination.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental results on dorsal bending bias.

claim: One function of AS MNs may be to facilitate navigation.
source: Thus, one function of AS MNs may be to facilitate navigation.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation based on the observed circular crawling behavior.

claim: AS MNs have no 'opposing' partner neurons (like VA/DA or VB/DB).
source: Unlike the A and B class MNs, the AS MNs have no 'opposing' partner neurons (like VA/DA or VB/DB) and innervate (dorsal) BWMs and inhibitory VD neurons (that innervate ventral muscle).
evidence: This is based on anatomical knowledge from the wiring diagram.

claim: AS MNs innervate dorsal BWMs and inhibitory VD neurons that innervate ventral muscle.
source: Unlike the A and B class MNs, the AS MNs have no 'opposing' partner neurons (like VA/DA or VB/DB) and innervate (dorsal) BWMs and inhibitory VD neurons (that innervate ventral muscle).
evidence: This is based on anatomical knowledge from the wiring diagram.

claim: Intrinsically evoked activity in muscle cells was not synchronized across animals.
source: We observed intrinsically evoked activity in muscle cells, that was not synchronized across animals, but which uncovered alternating dorso-ventral activity when the traces of both sides of the animals were aligned to the first dorsal peak (Figure 2BII, III, IV-VIII).
evidence: This is supported by calcium imaging data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Intrinsically evoked muscle activity uncovered alternating dorso-ventral activity when traces were aligned to the first dorsal peak.
source: We observed intrinsically evoked activity in muscle cells, that was not synchronized across animals, but which uncovered alternating dorso-ventral activity when the traces of both sides of the animals were aligned to the first dorsal peak (Figure 2BII, III, IV-VIII).
evidence: This is supported by calcium imaging data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Intrinsic muscle activity is likely evoked by the motor nervous system, even in an immobilized animal.
source: This activity is likely evoked by the motor nervous system, even in an immobilized animal.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observed muscle activity patterns.

claim: Photostimulation of AS MNs caused asymmetric responses in the BWM: Ca2+ signal in dorsal muscle cells increased, while it simultaneously decreased in the ventral muscles.
source: When we photostimulated (ChR2) AS MNs (Figure 2BII, IV-VI, and Figure 2—video 1) in animals raised with ATR, we observed asymmetric responses in the BWM: The Ca2+ signal in dorsal muscle cells increased, while it simultaneously decreased in the ventral muscles.
evidence: This is supported by calcium imaging data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The asymmetry in AS MNs anatomy is reflected by asymmetry of their functional output.
source: Thus, the asymmetry in AS MNs anatomy is reflected also by asymmetry of their functional output.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observed asymmetric muscle responses.

claim: Animals with ablated AS MNs retained the ability to move, but crawled with lower speed.
source: Brief illumination of the AS MNs with 470 nm light (2 mW/mm2, 2.5 min) led to visible and quantifiable locomotion defects: Animals with ablated AS MNs retained the ability to move, but crawled with lower speed, increased bending angles and an overall distorted undulation wave along the body, with a highly irregular pattern (Figure 3AII-IV, Figure 3—figure supplement 1A; Figure 3—video 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Animals with ablated AS MNs showed increased bending angles.
source: Brief illumination of the AS MNs with 470 nm light (2 mW/mm2, 2.5 min) led to visible and quantifiable locomotion defects: Animals with ablated AS MNs retained the ability to move, but crawled with lower speed, increased bending angles and an overall distorted undulation wave along the body, with a highly irregular pattern (Figure 3AII-IV, Figure 3—figure supplement 1A; Figure 3—video 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Animals with ablated AS MNs showed an overall distorted undulation wave along the body, with a highly irregular pattern.
source: Brief illumination of the AS MNs with 470 nm light (2 mW/mm2, 2.5 min) led to visible and quantifiable locomotion defects: Animals with ablated AS MNs retained the ability to move, but crawled with lower speed, increased bending angles and an overall distorted undulation wave along the body, with a highly irregular pattern (Figure 3AII-IV, Figure 3—figure supplement 1A; Figure 3—video 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Ablation of AS MNs disrupted coordination of the bending wave.
source: Thus, ablation of AS MNs disrupted coordination of the bending wave.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental results on AS MN ablation.

claim: After AS MN ablation, dorsal muscle showed higher fluorescence that was significantly reduced compared to ventral muscle.
source: Ventral muscles showed Ca2+ fluctuations that led to intermediate fluorescence when averaged over many animals, both in the presence, or after the ablation of AS MNs. In contrast, the dorsal muscle on average showed higher fluorescence that, upon AS MN ablation, was significantly reduced compared to ventral muscle (Figure 3AV-VII).
evidence: This is supported by calcium imaging data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: AS MNs provide biased dorsal muscle drive.
source: This emphasizes that AS MNs provide biased dorsal muscle drive.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the calcium imaging results after AS MN ablation.

claim: Animals expressing HisCl1 in AS MNs on histamine plates moved significantly slower (ca. 75% reduction) than animals without histamine.
source: Animals on histamine plates moved significantly slower (ca. 75% reduction) than animals without histamine, demonstrating that AS MNs are actively involved in promoting locomotion (however, this manipulation also affects other cholinergic neurons outside the VNC; see below).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: AS MNs are actively involved in promoting locomotion.
source: Animals on histamine plates moved significantly slower (ca. 75% reduction) than animals without histamine, demonstrating that AS MNs are actively involved in promoting locomotion (however, this manipulation also affects other cholinergic neurons outside the VNC; see below).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the HisCl1 experiment, with a caveat about specificity.

claim: Histamine exposure strongly disturbed the propagation of the body wave, leading to very slow and irregular movement and frequent directional changes.
source: Histamine exposure strongly disturbed the propagation of the body wave, leading to very slow and irregular movement and frequent directional changes.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: In animals with hyperpolarized AS MNs, intrinsically evoked Ca2+ activity was observed only in ventral BWM, and animals showed ventral bending.
source: Consistent with the dorsal innervation of muscles by AS MNs, intrinsically evoked Ca2+ activity in animals with hyperpolarized AS MNs was observed only in ventral BWM, and animals showed ventral bending.
evidence: This is supported by calcium imaging data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: On histamine, ventral Ca2+ fluctuations had much higher amplitude than those in dorsal muscle.
source: Over time, on histamine, ventral Ca2+ fluctuations had much higher amplitude than those in dorsal muscle, while animals without histamine showed comparable fluctuations in both dorsal and ventral muscles, which were of the same low amplitude as in dorsal muscle with histamine (Figure 3BV-VII).
evidence: This is supported by calcium imaging data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Hyperpolarization of AS MNs inhibits their excitatory signaling to dorsal muscles.
source: In sum, hyperpolarization of AS MNs inhibits their excitatory signaling to dorsal muscles, and blocks their activation of GABAergic VD motor neurons, which leads to ventral muscle disinhibition.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental results on AS MN hyperpolarization.

claim: Hyperpolarization of AS MNs blocks their activation of GABAergic VD motor neurons, which leads to ventral muscle disinhibition.
source: In sum, hyperpolarization of AS MNs inhibits their excitatory signaling to dorsal muscles, and blocks their activation of GABAergic VD motor neurons, which leads to ventral muscle disinhibition.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental results on AS MN hyperpolarization.

claim: Both ablation and hyperpolarization of AS MNs cause a strong bias to uniform ventral muscle activation, which is likely to disrupt propagation of the body wave.
source: Similar effects are found upon ablation of AS MNs, and both types of manipulation cause a strong bias to uniform ventral muscle activation, which is likely to disrupt propagation of the body wave.
evidence: This is an interpretation comparing the effects of ablation and hyperpolarization.

claim: Acute, ACR1-induced photo-hyperpolarization of all cholinergic neurons in freely moving animals strongly reduced crawling speed (to below 20%) and essentially stopped locomotion.
source: Acute, ACR1-induced photo-hyperpolarization of all cholinergic neurons in freely moving animals strongly reduced crawling speed (to below 20%) and essentially stopped locomotion (Figure 4B,C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4B and 4C.

claim: When expression of ACR1 and illumination were restricted to the AS MNs, a similar reduction of speed was observed (to ca. 35% of the initial speed), though not as pronounced as for all cholinergic neurons.
source: When we restricted expression of ACR1 and illumination to the AS MNs, we observed a similar reduction of speed, though not as pronounced (to ca. 35% of the initial speed; Figure 4B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Hyperpolarization of only the AS MNs led to partial and transient body contraction.
source: However, hyperpolarization of only the AS MNs led to partial and transient body contraction (Figure 4C; Figure 4—video 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Body contraction from AS MN hyperpolarization might be explained by synaptic connections of AS MNs to the GABAergic VD MNs: Hyperpolarization of AS MNs would reduce excitation of VD MNs, which in turn would cause dis-inhibition of muscle cells, and thus contraction.
source: This might be explained by synaptic connections of AS MNs to the GABAergic VD MNs: Hyperpolarization of AS MNs would reduce excitation of VD MNs, which in turn would cause dis-inhibition of muscle cells, and thus contraction.
evidence: This is a mechanistic interpretation of the observed body contraction.

claim: unc-47 mutants showed relaxation instead of contraction of BWMs upon AS MN hyperpolarization.
source: To test this, we repeated the experiment in unc-47(e307) mutants, lacking the vesicular GABA transporter, and thus GABAergic transmission. Consistently, unc-47 mutants showed relaxation instead of contraction of BWMs (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4C, testing the mechanistic hypothesis.

claim: Body wave propagation was strongly attenuated by AS MN hyperpolarization using ACR1.
source: Body wave propagation was strongly attenuated, as for the analogous experiment using HisCl1 in AS MNs; however, using ACR1, this was induced within 2 – 3 s of illumination.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data comparing ACR1 and HisCl1 experiments.

claim: In about half of the animals tested, inhibition of anterior and midbody AS neurons hindered propagation of the wave to the posterior part of the body, leading to dragging behind of the tail region.
source: This was the case: In about half of the animals tested, inhibition of anterior and midbody AS neurons hindered propagation of the wave to the posterior part of the body, leading to dragging behind of the tail region (Figure 4D; Figure 4—video 2-4).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: The extent of reduction in body movement in the anterior part of the animal was significantly smaller than the change in posterior body movement when midbody AS neurons were inhibited.
source: Analyses of the extent of movement in individual body segments showed that a reduction of movement was also found in the head region, however, this was more pronounced toward the posterior, particularly when the midbody AS neurons were inhibited (Figure 4E; Figure 4—figure supplement 1A shows how the eleven 3-point angles analyzed correspond to illuminated body segments): The extent of reduction in body movement in the anterior part of the animal was significantly smaller than the change in posterior body movement (Figure 4F).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4E and 4F.

claim: AS MNs are required for antero-posterior propagation of the body wave.
source: In sum, AS MNs are required for antero-posterior propagation of the body wave.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental results on segmental AS MN inhibition.

claim: Correlation of Ca2+ traces in AS MNs with dorsal body bends was previously shown in freely crawling animals.
source: Correlation of Ca2+ traces in AS MNs with dorsal body bends was previously shown in freely crawling animals (Faumont et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: AS6 and AS7 showed oscillatory activity during locomotion, which was correlated with the change of body bends.
source: AS6 and AS7 showed oscillatory activity during locomotion, which was correlated with the change of body bends.
evidence: This is supported by calcium imaging data in moving animals shown in Figure 5.

claim: During forward crawling, (anterior) AS6 activity preceded (posterior) AS7 activity by about 1–2 s.
source: During forward crawling, (anterior) AS6 activity preceded (posterior) AS7 activity by about 1–2 s (Figure 5A,B; Figure 5—video 1).
evidence: This is supported by calcium imaging data shown in Figure 5.

claim: The Ca2+ signal in AS6 preceded the maximal bending at the vulva by about 2 s.
source: Here, the Ca2+ signal in AS6 preceded the maximal bending at the vulva by about 2 s, while the signal in AS7 coincided (correlation coefficients were ~0.30–0.35).
evidence: This is supported by cross-correlation analysis shown in Figure 5D.

claim: The Ca2+ signal in AS7 coincided with maximal bending at the vulva.
source: Here, the Ca2+ signal in AS6 preceded the maximal bending at the vulva by about 2 s, while the signal in AS7 coincided (correlation coefficients were ~0.30–0.35).
evidence: This is supported by cross-correlation analysis shown in Figure 5D.

claim: The wave of activity in AS MNs appears to travel antero-posteriorly at the time scale of the undulatory wave.
source: Thus, the wave of activity in AS MNs appears to travel antero-posteriorly at the time scale of the undulatory wave.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the temporal relationships observed in calcium imaging.

claim: During reversal periods, there was weaker correlation (coefficient ~0.15–0.3) of AS6 and AS7 Ca2+ signals with the vulva bending angles, or with each other.
source: During reversal periods (we only included reversals of at least 10 s; Figure 5C), there was weaker correlation (coefficient ~0.15–0.3) of AS6 and AS7 Ca2+ signals with the vulva bending angles, or with each other, and there was a smaller time lag between these signals (~1 s, Figure 5E).
evidence: This is supported by cross-correlation analysis shown in Figure 5E.

claim: The cross-correlation of Ca2+ signals of the neurons and the bending angle were not different between forward and reversal locomotion.
source: The cross-correlation of Ca2+ signals of the neurons and the bending angle were not different between forward and reversal locomotion (Figure 5F).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis shown in Figure 5F.

claim: The peaks of AS6 and AS7 Ca2+ signals did not reveal any difference between forward and reverse movements.
source: The peaks of AS6 and AS7 Ca2+ signals did not reveal any difference between forward and reverse movements (Figure 5G).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis shown in Figure 5G.

claim: AS MNs showed oscillatory activity that was correlated with body bends during both forward and backward crawling.
source: In sum, AS MNs showed oscillatory activity that was correlated with body bends during both forward and backward crawling.
evidence: This is a summary interpretation of the calcium imaging results in moving animals.

claim: The PINs AVA, AVD, and AVE connect to the DA and VA MNs, and induce reversals and backward locomotion.
source: The PINs AVA, AVD, and AVE connect to the DA and VA MNs, and induce reversals and backward locomotion.
evidence: This is established knowledge about C. elegans locomotor circuits.

claim: The PINs AVB and PVC are connected to the DB and VB forward MNs and mediate forward locomotion.
source: Conversely, the PINs AVB and PVC are connected to the DB and VB forward MNs and mediate forward locomotion (Chalfie et al., 1985; Chronis et al., 2007; Kawano et al., 2011; Piggott et al., 2011; Qi et al., 2013; Wicks et al., 1996).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Endogenous as well as stimulated activity of the PINs modulates activity of A- and B-type MNs.
source: Endogenous (Kawano et al., 2011) as well as stimulated activity of the PINs modulates activity of A- and B-type MNs (Gao et al., 2015; Gao et al., 2018; Liu et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: The AS MNs are postsynaptic to both backward PINs (synapse number: AVA - 63, AVE - 7) and forward PINs (AVB - 13, PVC - 2).
source: The AS MNs are postsynaptic to both backward (synapse number: AVA - 63, AVE - 7) and forward PINs (AVB - 13, PVC - 2).
evidence: This is based on the wiring diagram from previous anatomical studies.

claim: There are 37 gap junctions reported between AVA and the AS MNs.
source: No chemical synapses are known from AS MNs towards the PINs, yet, there are 37 gap junctions reported between AVA and the AS MNs as well as five gap junctions between AVB and the AS MNs.
evidence: This is based on the wiring diagram from previous anatomical studies.

claim: There are five gap junctions between AVB and the AS MNs.
source: No chemical synapses are known from AS MNs towards the PINs, yet, there are 37 gap junctions reported between AVA and the AS MNs as well as five gap junctions between AVB and the AS MNs.
evidence: This is based on the wiring diagram from previous anatomical studies.

claim: Electrical synapses could mediate anterograde as well as retrograde signaling between AS MNs and PINs.
source: Electrical synapses could mediate anterograde as well as retrograde signaling between AS MNs and PINs (Chen et al., 2006; Varshney et al., 2011; White et al., 1986).
evidence: This is a general statement about the properties of electrical synapses, with citations.

claim: Stimulation of AVA or AVB both resulted in a steady, synchronous increase of the Ca2+ signal in the AS3 neuron.
source: Stimulation of AVA or AVB both resulted in a steady, synchronous increase of the Ca2+ signal in the AS3 neuron; however, no increase was observed in animals raised without ATR (Figure 6AII-IV; Figure 6—video 1, 2).
evidence: This is supported by calcium imaging data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: A similar increase was found in the AS8 neuron, and both AS3 and AS8 showed a synchronized increase of activity upon PIN stimulation.
source: A similar increase was found in the AS8 neuron, and both AS3 and AS8 showed a synchronized increase of activity (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A,B).
evidence: This is supported by calcium imaging data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: Signaling from both forward and backward PINs is excitatory to the AS MNs.
source: Thus, signaling from both forward and backward PINs is excitatory to the AS MNs.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the calcium imaging results showing increased AS MN activity upon PIN stimulation.

claim: AVA depolarization evoked a response of comparably low amplitude (20% ΔF/F after 3 s) in AS MNs.
source: While AVA depolarization evoked a response of comparably low, and AVB depolarization caused a response of significantly higher amplitude (20 vs. 40% ΔF/F after 3 s, respectively; Figure 6AIV), this difference is probably not meaningful, as expression levels of ChR2 in AVA vs. in AVB likely differ.
evidence: This is supported by calcium imaging data shown in Figure 6A, with a caveat about interpretation.

claim: AVB depolarization caused a response of significantly higher amplitude (40% ΔF/F after 3 s) in AS MNs.
source: While AVA depolarization evoked a response of comparably low, and AVB depolarization caused a response of significantly higher amplitude (20 vs. 40% ΔF/F after 3 s, respectively; Figure 6AIV), this difference is probably not meaningful, as expression levels of ChR2 in AVA vs. in AVB likely differ.
evidence: This is supported by calcium imaging data shown in Figure 6A, with a caveat about interpretation.

claim: The difference in AS MN response amplitude between AVA and AVB stimulation is probably not meaningful, as expression levels of ChR2 in AVA vs. in AVB likely differ.
source: While AVA depolarization evoked a response of comparably low, and AVB depolarization caused a response of significantly higher amplitude (20 vs. 40% ΔF/F after 3 s, respectively; Figure 6AIV), this difference is probably not meaningful, as expression levels of ChR2 in AVA vs. in AVB likely differ.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation acknowledging a technical limitation.

claim: Inequality in regulated behavior based on imbalances in wiring has been observed for the PINs and A- and B-class MNs.
source: Inequality in regulated behavior based on imbalances in wiring has been observed for the PINs and A- and B-class MNs (Kawano et al., 2011; Roberts et al., 2016), where AVA coupling to A-type MNs via gap junctions is rectifying towards AVA (Liu et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: AVA coupling to A-type MNs via gap junctions is rectifying towards AVA.
source: Inequality in regulated behavior based on imbalances in wiring has been observed for the PINs and A- and B-class MNs (Kawano et al., 2011; Roberts et al., 2016), where AVA coupling to A-type MNs via gap junctions is rectifying towards AVA (Liu et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: AS MNs express UNC-7 and INX-3 as the sole innexins.
source: AS MNs express UNC-7 and INX-3 as the sole innexins.
evidence: This is based on known expression patterns of innexins.

claim: INX-3 is widely expressed in multiple tissues.
source: INX-3 is widely expressed in multiple tissues, and AVA and AVB also express UNC-7 (Altun et al., 2009; Starich et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work on innexin expression.

claim: AVA and AVB also express UNC-7.
source: INX-3 is widely expressed in multiple tissues, and AVA and AVB also express UNC-7 (Altun et al., 2009; Starich et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work on innexin expression.

claim: In unc-7(e5) null mutant, no electrical coupling should occur between AS MNs and AVA or AVB.
source: Thus, we used an unc-7(e5) null mutant, in which no electrical coupling should occur between AS MNs and AVA or AVB, and repeated the above experiments (Figure 6BI-IV).
evidence: This is an inference based on the known function of UNC-7 in gap junctions.

claim: In unc-7 mutants, AVB stimulation showed similar depolarization of AS MNs as in wild type.
source: This showed similar depolarization of AS MNs following AVB stimulation, while activity of the AS MNs did not increase significantly with ATR.
evidence: This is supported by calcium imaging data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Gap junctions may contribute particularly to AVA-AS MN signaling.
source: Thus, gap junctions may contribute particularly to AVA-AS MN signaling.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the unc-7 mutant results, with speculative language.

claim: Photodepolarization of the AS MNs caused Ca2+ transients in AVA (ΔR/R ~ 18%).
source: Photodepolarization of the AS MNs (in animals raised in the presence of ATR) caused Ca2+ transients in AVA (ΔR/R ~ 18%), but had no significant effect on Ca2+activity in AVB interneurons (Figure 6CII-IV).
evidence: This is supported by calcium imaging data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: Photodepolarization of the AS MNs had no significant effect on Ca2+ activity in AVB interneurons.
source: Photodepolarization of the AS MNs (in animals raised in the presence of ATR) caused Ca2+ transients in AVA (ΔR/R ~ 18%), but had no significant effect on Ca2+activity in AVB interneurons (Figure 6CII-IV).
evidence: This is supported by calcium imaging data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: The lack of effect on AVB is in line with the much smaller number of gap junctions between AS MNs and AVB.
source: The latter is in line with the much smaller number of gap junctions between AS MNs and AVB.
evidence: This is an interpretation relating the functional result to anatomical connectivity.

claim: In the unc-7 gap junction mutant background, the Ca2+ signal in AVA (ΔR/R ~ 11%) was comparable to the signal observed in the control without ATR.
source: In the unc-7 gap junction mutant background, the Ca2+ signal (ΔR/R ~ 11%) was now comparable to the signal observed in the control without ATR, indicating that UNC-7 electrical synapses are responsible for transmission between AS MNs and AVA.
evidence: This is supported by calcium imaging data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: UNC-7 electrical synapses are responsible for transmission between AS MNs and AVA.
source: In the unc-7 gap junction mutant background, the Ca2+ signal (ΔR/R ~ 11%) was now comparable to the signal observed in the control without ATR, indicating that UNC-7 electrical synapses are responsible for transmission between AS MNs and AVA.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the unc-7 mutant results.

claim: AS MNs occupy a significant part of the VNC circuit (11 of 75 neurons).
source: AS MNs occupy a significant part of the VNC circuit (11 of 75 neurons) and two AS MNs are present in each functional segment of the circuit (Haspel and O'Donovan, 2011).
evidence: This is based on anatomical knowledge with citation.

claim: Two AS MNs are present in each functional segment of the circuit.
source: AS MNs occupy a significant part of the VNC circuit (11 of 75 neurons) and two AS MNs are present in each functional segment of the circuit (Haspel and O'Donovan, 2011).
evidence: This is based on anatomical knowledge with citation.

claim: In absence of physiological information, AS MNs were missing in many models representing the locomotor circuit function in C. elegans.
source: Yet, in absence of physiological information, they were missing in many models representing the locomotor circuit function in C. elegans (Von Stetina et al., 2005; Zhen and Samuel, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous modeling work.

claim: AS MNs are important for several aspects of locomotion, among them dorso-ventral coordination.
source: We showed that AS MNs are important for several aspects of locomotion, among them dorso-ventral coordination: Their depolarization activates dorsal BWMs leading to contraction and dorsal bias in freely moving animals, while AS MN hyperpolarization eliminates activity in dorsal BWMs and induces contraction of ventral BWMs through disinhibition.
evidence: This is a summary of the main findings from the study.

claim: AS MN depolarization activates dorsal BWMs leading to contraction and dorsal bias in freely moving animals.
source: We showed that AS MNs are important for several aspects of locomotion, among them dorso-ventral coordination: Their depolarization activates dorsal BWMs leading to contraction and dorsal bias in freely moving animals, while AS MN hyperpolarization eliminates activity in dorsal BWMs and induces contraction of ventral BWMs through disinhibition.
evidence: This is a summary of experimental findings.

claim: AS MN hyperpolarization eliminates activity in dorsal BWMs and induces contraction of ventral BWMs through disinhibition.
source: We showed that AS MNs are important for several aspects of locomotion, among them dorso-ventral coordination: Their depolarization activates dorsal BWMs leading to contraction and dorsal bias in freely moving animals, while AS MN hyperpolarization eliminates activity in dorsal BWMs and induces contraction of ventral BWMs through disinhibition.
evidence: This is a summary of experimental findings.

claim: It is likely that AS MNs counteract neurons providing a ventral bias, e.g. the VA and VB MNs, or even the VC neurons.
source: Thus, it is likely that AS MNs counteract neurons providing a ventral bias, e.g. the VA and VB MNs, or even the VC neurons (Faumont et al., 2011; White et al., 1986).
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation based on the observed dorsal bias and known anatomy.

claim: Recent computational studies predicted a significant role of AS MNs in coordinating dorso-ventral bending.
source: This corresponds to recent computational studies, which predicted a significant role of AS MNs in coordinating dorso-ventral bending (Olivares et al., 2017) and in the control of BWMs (Yan et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to computational modeling work.

claim: Recent computational studies predicted a significant role of AS MNs in the control of BWMs.
source: This corresponds to recent computational studies, which predicted a significant role of AS MNs in coordinating dorso-ventral bending (Olivares et al., 2017) and in the control of BWMs (Yan et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to computational modeling work.

claim: AS MNs are active both during forward and reverse locomotion.
source: Furthermore, AS MNs are active both during forward and reverse locomotion.
evidence: This is a summary of calcium imaging findings in moving animals.

claim: AS MNs could play a role in integrating forward and backward locomotion motifs.
source: Since the AS MNs connect to both forward and backward PINs, they could play a role in integrating forward and backward locomotion motifs, e.g. by providing an electrical sink (or source; this is more likely for AS-to-AVA signaling, due to the higher number of gap junctions, and in line with our results) for the PINs of the respective opposite direction (Figure 7A,B).
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the connectivity and functional data.

claim: Similar functions were shown for A-type MNs and AVA as well as for V2a interneurons and MNs in zebrafish.
source: Similar functions were shown for A-type MNs and AVA (Kawano et al., 2011; Liu et al., 2017) as well as for V2a interneurons and MNs in zebrafish (Song et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work in C. elegans and zebrafish.

claim: Optogenetic depolarization of AS MNs, resulting in curved locomotion tracks, mimicked the 'weathervane' mode of navigation towards a source of attractive salt.
source: Indeed, optogenetic depolarization of AS MNs, resulting in curved locomotion tracks, mimicked the 'weathervane' mode of navigation towards a source of attractive salt (Iino and Yoshida, 2009).
evidence: This is an interpretation relating the experimental results to a known navigation behavior, with citation.

claim: In the lamprey, lateral bends were caused by asymmetry in stimulation of the mesencephalic locomotor region.
source: In the lamprey, lateral bends were caused by asymmetry in stimulation of the mesencephalic locomotor region (Sirota et al., 2000), and in the freely moving lamprey even comparatively small left or right asymmetries in activity of the reticulospinal system correspond to lateral turning (Deliagina et al., 2000).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work on lamprey locomotion.

claim: In the freely moving lamprey, even comparatively small left or right asymmetries in activity of the reticulospinal system correspond to lateral turning.
source: In the lamprey, lateral bends were caused by asymmetry in stimulation of the mesencephalic locomotor region (Sirota et al., 2000), and in the freely moving lamprey even comparatively small left or right asymmetries in activity of the reticulospinal system correspond to lateral turning (Deliagina et al., 2000).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work on lamprey locomotion.

claim: Asymmetry in contralateral motifs of complex locomotor circuits is also known from vertebrate spinal cord CPGs in flexor-extensor coordination.
source: Asymmetry in contralateral motifs of complex locomotor circuits is also known from vertebrate spinal cord CPGs in flexor-extensor coordination (Grillner and Wallén, 2002).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work on vertebrate CPGs.

claim: In mice, flexor motor neurons are predominantly active and inhibit extensor motor neurons, which in turn show intervals of tonic activity between inhibitory states, corresponding to flexor bursts.
source: In mice, flexor motor neurons are predominantly active and inhibit extensor motor neurons, which in turn show intervals of tonic activity between inhibitory states, corresponding to flexor bursts (Machado et al., 2015; Rybak et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work on mouse locomotor circuits.

claim: When comparing numbers of synaptic inputs from C. elegans cholinergic MNs to BWM, predominance is apparent in excitatory neuromuscular junctions from A- and B-type MNs to ventral muscles.
source: When comparing numbers of synaptic inputs from C. elegans cholinergic MNs to BWM (Varshney et al., 2011; White et al., 1986), predominance is apparent in excitatory neuromuscular junctions from A- and B-type MNs to ventral muscles (number of synapses: A-type to ventral muscle: 225, to dorsal muscle: 111, B-type to ventral muscle: 228, to dorsal muscle: 58), as well as in the corresponding contralateral synapses to inhibitory DD MNs, which innervate dorsal muscle (VA and VB to DD: 180 and 194 synapses, DA and DB to DD: 8 and 29 synapses).
evidence: This is based on synapse counts from the wiring diagram, with citations.

claim: Tonic activity of B- or A-type MNs would be expected to generate a bias towards ventral bending, and this could be balanced by excitation of AS MNs.
source: Therefore, tonic activity of B- or A-type MNs would be expected to generate a bias towards ventral bending, and this could be balanced by excitation of AS MNs.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation based on synapse counts and functional data.

claim: VC neurons may contribute in counteracting AS MN function.
source: In addition, VC neurons may contribute in counteracting AS MN function (see above).
evidence: This is a speculative statement about potential circuit interactions.

claim: The compressed nature of the C. elegans nervous system, in which single neurons fulfill multiple tasks that in higher animals are executed by layers of different cells, may not always allow for the direct comparison to vertebrate systems.
source: However, the compressed nature of the C. elegans nervous system, in which single neurons fulfill multiple tasks that in higher animals are executed by layers of different cells, may not always allow for the direct comparison to vertebrate systems.
evidence: This is a general statement about limitations of comparing C. elegans to vertebrate systems.

claim: The groups of forward (AVB, PVC) and backward PINs (AVA, AVD, AVE), respectively, are synchronized.
source: The groups of forward (AVB, PVC) and backward PINs (AVA, AVD, AVE), respectively, are synchronized (Prevedel et al., 2014), inhibit each other and change their state stochastically (Pierce-Shimomura et al., 2008; Roberts et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Forward and backward PINs inhibit each other and change their state stochastically.
source: The groups of forward (AVB, PVC) and backward PINs (AVA, AVD, AVE), respectively, are synchronized (Prevedel et al., 2014), inhibit each other and change their state stochastically (Pierce-Shimomura et al., 2008; Roberts et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Ability of MNs to modulate activity of PINs was shown for B-type MNs changing the inhibitory chemical transmission of AVB to AVA in C. elegans.
source: Recently, ability of MNs to modulate activity of PINs was shown in several animal models: for B-type MNs changing the inhibitory chemical transmission of AVB to AVA in C. elegans (Kawano et al., 2011; Liu et al., 2017), for MNs regulating the frequency of crawling in Drosophila (Matsunaga et al., 2017), for MNs affecting activity of the excitatory V2a neurons in zebrafish (Song et al., 2016), and, in mice, such activity was suggested for MNs, changing the frequency of rhythmic CPG activity after stimulation by rhodopsins (Falgairolle et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: MNs regulate the frequency of crawling in Drosophila.
source: Recently, ability of MNs to modulate activity of PINs was shown in several animal models: for B-type MNs changing the inhibitory chemical transmission of AVB to AVA in C. elegans (Kawano et al., 2011; Liu et al., 2017), for MNs regulating the frequency of crawling in Drosophila (Matsunaga et al., 2017), for MNs affecting activity of the excitatory V2a neurons in zebrafish (Song et al., 2016), and, in mice, such activity was suggested for MNs, changing the frequency of rhythmic CPG activity after stimulation by rhodopsins (Falgairolle et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: MNs affect activity of the excitatory V2a neurons in zebrafish.
source: Recently, ability of MNs to modulate activity of PINs was shown in several animal models: for B-type MNs changing the inhibitory chemical transmission of AVB to AVA in C. elegans (Kawano et al., 2011; Liu et al., 2017), for MNs regulating the frequency of crawling in Drosophila (Matsunaga et al., 2017), for MNs affecting activity of the excitatory V2a neurons in zebrafish (Song et al., 2016), and, in mice, such activity was suggested for MNs, changing the frequency of rhythmic CPG activity after stimulation by rhodopsins (Falgairolle et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: In mice, MNs were suggested to change the frequency of rhythmic CPG activity after stimulation by rhodopsins.
source: Recently, ability of MNs to modulate activity of PINs was shown in several animal models: for B-type MNs changing the inhibitory chemical transmission of AVB to AVA in C. elegans (Kawano et al., 2011; Liu et al., 2017), for MNs regulating the frequency of crawling in Drosophila (Matsunaga et al., 2017), for MNs affecting activity of the excitatory V2a neurons in zebrafish (Song et al., 2016), and, in mice, such activity was suggested for MNs, changing the frequency of rhythmic CPG activity after stimulation by rhodopsins (Falgairolle et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work, with speculative language ('suggested').

claim: Positive feedback from MNs required the function of gap junctions, coupling between MNs and PINs in all these systems.
source: Positive feedback from MNs required the function of gap junctions, coupling between MNs and PINs in all these systems.
evidence: This is a general statement about the mechanism of MN feedback across multiple systems.

claim: Our data suggest that AS MNs have electrical feedback to the backward PIN AVA.
source: Our data suggest that AS MNs have electrical feedback to the backward PIN AVA.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the experimental results, with speculative language.

claim: If the AS neurons would provide inhibition in the context of the free moving animal, e.g. as an electrical sink for AVA, AS MN activity may exert a bias to promote the forward locomotion state.
source: If the AS neurons would provide inhibition in the context of the free moving animal, e.g. as an electrical sink for AVA, AS MN activity may exert a bias to promote the forward locomotion state.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the potential functional role of AS MNs.

claim: CPGs are dedicated neural circuits with intrinsic rhythmic activities.
source: CPGs are dedicated neural circuits with intrinsic rhythmic activities (Grillner, 2006; Guertin, 2012).
evidence: This is a definition supported by citations.

claim: In many organisms including those showing undulatory movement (e.g. leech, lamprey), series of CPGs are distributed along the length of the body in locomotor neural circuits.
source: In many organisms including those showing undulatory movement (e.g. leech, lamprey), series of CPGs are distributed along the length of the body in locomotor neural circuits (Kristan et al., 2005; Mullins et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: In C. elegans, the bending wave can be generated even in the absence of all PINs.
source: In C. elegans, the bending wave can be generated even in the absence of all PINs (Gao et al., 2018; Kawano et al., 2011; Zheng et al., 1999) as well as in absence of GABAergic MNs (Donnelly et al., 2013; McIntire et al., 1993).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: In C. elegans, the bending wave can be generated in absence of GABAergic MNs.
source: In C. elegans, the bending wave can be generated even in the absence of all PINs (Gao et al., 2018; Kawano et al., 2011; Zheng et al., 1999) as well as in absence of GABAergic MNs (Donnelly et al., 2013; McIntire et al., 1993).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: The existence of series of CPGs in the C. elegans VNC was discussed for a long time, and single neurons or small groups of neurons were suggested.
source: The existence of series of CPGs in the C. elegans VNC was discussed for a long time, and single neurons or small groups of neurons were suggested (Cohen and Sanders, 2014; Gjorgjieva et al., 2014; Zhen and Samuel, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: B-type MNs are able to propagate the bending wave posteriorly.
source: B-type MNs are able to propagate the bending wave posteriorly.
evidence: This is established knowledge about B-type MN function.

claim: The bending may originate from a possible head CPG that generates head oscillations.
source: The bending may originate from a possible head CPG that generates head oscillations (Hendricks et al., 2012; Shen et al., 2016), simply by proprioceptive coupling (Wen et al., 2012), though recent work showed that also gap junctions are involved (Xu et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work, with speculative language.

claim: Pacemaker properties of the posterior A-type MN, DA9, were revealed during backward locomotion, that are based on the activity of a P/Q/N-type Ca2+ channel.
source: Recently, pacemaker properties of the posterior A-type MN, DA9, were revealed during backward locomotion, that are based on the activity of a P/Q/N-type Ca2+ channel (Gao et al., 2018), and local oscillators were shown to function in the VNC also for forward locomotion (Fouad et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Local oscillators were shown to function in the VNC also for forward locomotion.
source: Recently, pacemaker properties of the posterior A-type MN, DA9, were revealed during backward locomotion, that are based on the activity of a P/Q/N-type Ca2+ channel (Gao et al., 2018), and local oscillators were shown to function in the VNC also for forward locomotion (Fouad et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Computational modelling of repeating units of the VNC identified a dorsally oriented sub-circuit consisting of AS, DA, and DB MNs, which could act as a potential CPG.
source: Computational modelling of repeating units of the VNC (Haspel and O'Donovan, 2011), based on connectome data, identified a dorsally oriented sub-circuit consisting of AS, DA, and DB MNs, which could act as a potential CPG (Olivares et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to computational modeling work.

claim: Recording dorso-ventral and temporally coordinated oscillatory muscle Ca2+ transients in immobilized animals may be a consequence of rhythmic activity in the motor nervous system.
source: Our data on recording dorso-ventral and temporally coordinated oscillatory muscle Ca2+ transients in immobilized animals may be a consequence of rhythmic activity in the motor nervous system.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the observed muscle activity.

claim: Whether AS MNs are part of rhythmic activity in the motor nervous system is currently unknown.
source: Yet, whether AS MNs are part of this activity is currently unknown.
evidence: This acknowledges a limitation of the current study.

claim: The oscillations of AS MN Ca2+ levels observed during forward and reverse locomotion are not per se an indication of pacemaker activity, as they may be affected by proprioceptive feedback or through other motor neurons.
source: The oscillations of AS MN Ca2+ levels we observed both during forward and reverse locomotion are not per se an indication of pacemaker activity, as they may be affected by proprioceptive feedback or through other motor neurons.
evidence: This is a cautious interpretation of the calcium imaging results.

claim: AS MN oscillations were not observed in immobilized animals, which would have been a stronger indication of autonomous CPG activity.
source: We did not observe them in immobilized animals, which would have been a stronger indication of autonomous CPG activity.
evidence: This is a statement about what was not observed in the experiments.

claim: Among PINs, AVB and AVA are most important for enabling forward and backward locomotion, respectively.
source: Among PINs, AVB and AVA are most important for enabling forward and backward locomotion, respectively (Chalfie et al., 1985; Kato et al., 2015; Roberts et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Bistable states with two distinct membrane potentials, i.e. up and down states, that 'gate' activity of the downstream target neurons, were shown for several interneurons including AVA and AVB.
source: Bistable states with two distinct membrane potentials, i.e. up and down states, that 'gate' activity of the downstream target neurons, were shown for several interneurons including AVA and AVB (Gordus et al., 2015; Kato et al., 2015; Mellem et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: For MNs, bistability was inferred for the A-, B- and D- types of MNs from direct recordings.
source: For MNs, bistability was inferred for the A-, B- and D- types of MNs from direct recordings (Liu et al., 2014) as well as from the graded responses in muscles, corresponding to shorter or longer activity bursts in MNs (Liu et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: All-or-none responses in BWM cells, corresponding to spiking neurons as well as to mammalian skeletal muscles, that result from integrating graded excitatory and inhibitory input from MNs, were demonstrated.
source: Further, all-or-none responses in BWM cells, corresponding to spiking neurons as well as to mammalian skeletal muscles, that result from integrating graded excitatory and inhibitory input from MNs, were demonstrated (Gao and Zhen, 2011; Liu et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: AS MNs may integrate inputs from forward and backward PINs, or themselves influence the PINs via UNC-7 and/or INX-3 gap junctions, to gate signal propagation in the VNC during forward locomotion.
source: AS MNs may similarly integrate inputs from forward and backward PINs, or themselves influence the PINs via UNC-7 and/or INX-3 gap junctions, to gate signal propagation in the VNC during forward locomotion, or to couple to A-type MN oscillators (DA9), via the AVA PIN during backward locomotion (Gao et al., 2018).
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of AS MN function.

claim: AS MNs may couple to A-type MN oscillators (DA9), via the AVA PIN during backward locomotion.
source: AS MNs may similarly integrate inputs from forward and backward PINs, or themselves influence the PINs via UNC-7 and/or INX-3 gap junctions, to gate signal propagation in the VNC during forward locomotion, or to couple to A-type MN oscillators (DA9), via the AVA PIN during backward locomotion (Gao et al., 2018).
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation with citation to previous work on DA9.

claim: We found ceasing of locomotion when AS MNs were hyperpolarized, in line with the hypothesis that AS MNs gate signal propagation.
source: In line with this hypothesis, we found ceasing of locomotion when AS MNs were hyperpolarized.
evidence: This is an interpretation relating experimental results to a hypothesis.

claim: Gating neurons that affect rhythmic properties of CPGs are also known for the leech locomotor circuit.
source: Gating neurons that affect rhythmic properties of CPGs are also known for the leech locomotor circuit (Friesen and Kristan, 2007; Mullins et al., 2011; Taylor et al., 2000).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work on leech.

claim: The previously uncharacterized class of AS motor neurons is specialized in coordination of dorso-ventral undulation bends during wave propagation.
source: The previously uncharacterized class of AS motor neurons is specialized in coordination of dorso-ventral undulation bends during wave propagation, a feature maintained by asymmetry in both synaptic input and output.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion of the study.

claim: AS neuron specialization in coordination is maintained by asymmetry in both synaptic input and output.

claim: AS neurons integrate signals for forward and reverse locomotion from premotor interneurons.
source: Moreover AS neurons integrate signals for forward and reverse locomotion from premotor interneurons and potentially gate ventral nerve cord circuits and PINs via gap junctions.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion of the study.

claim: AS neurons potentially gate ventral nerve cord circuits and PINs via gap junctions.

claim: AS MNs send 68/144 documented synapses to the dorsal BWM cells (i.e. 47% of all presynaptic contacts made by the AS neurons).
source: According to the wiring diagram (Chen et al., 2006; Varshney et al., 2011; White et al., 1986) AS MNs send 68/144 documented synapses to the dorsal BWM cells (i.e. 47% of all presynaptic contacts made by the AS neurons) and 66/144 synapses to inhibitory ventral (GABAergic) VD MNs (i.e. 46% of all AS neuron synaptic terminals).
evidence: This is based on synapse counts from the wiring diagram, with citations.
